core.text: Someone described by what they are about to do, or intend to do, gets **the future participle (the 'about to' word: venturus = about to come)**: *epistulam scrīptūrus sum* — I am about to write a letter; *mīlitēs pugnātūrī* — soldiers about to fight. It is the participle stem with -ūr- slipped in before -us -a -um, and it is active. Latin name: *participium futūrī āctīvī*.
English has no single word for it; we say *about to …*, *going to …*, *on the point of …*.
Participle stem + -ūr- + -us -a -um. With sum it makes a near future: factūrus sum = I am going to do.

invented.en: The soldiers, about to fight, take up their swords.

core.text: *Scrīptus* is **the perfect participle (the 'having been done' word: laudatus = praised)**, passive and past; *scrīptūrus* is active and future. The -ūr- is the whole difference: *laudātus* — praised; *laudātūrus* — about to praise.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 23) list the three participles in a grid: present active -ns, perfect passive -tus, future active -ūrus (and the future passive, the gerundive, -ndus). Their examples: *puer ambulātūrus*, *oppidum cāsūrum*, *puella flōrem carptūra*, *mīlitēs moritūrī*. A deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks) forms it the same way and it is active as usual: *profectūrus* — about to set out.
*Sum* has *futūrus* — about to be, the future (adjective *futūrus* = future). The participle with *eram* gives 'was going to': *petītūrus eram tabernam* — I was intending to go to the shop.
